newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE-China steel plant teaches state firms to walk.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-China steel plant teaches state firms to walk.

text.p: If legend is any guide, those who come to learn from the residents of northern China's Handan city have not always benefited from the experience.

According to an ancient Chinese morality tale, one visitor keen to study the elegant Handan walking style not only failed to master it, but in the process forgot his own native gait and had to crawl home.

Dusty parables on the dangers of incomplete study have not deterred China's economic mandarins from ordering the entire nation's struggling state sector to learn from Handan Iron & Steel Group Co on how to stride into the new market economy.
Handan Iron & Steel, known in China as Hangang, has been named the official model for bloated state firms trying to end years of gross inefficiency, sliding sales and soaring costs.

Hangang officials say their company policy of "Simulated Market Accounting and Implementing Cost Vetoes" steered the steelworks from near-losses to solid profits in just five years -- and that others can learn from their success.
HANGANG WIELDS THE BIG VETO

Under the policy, Hangang managers applied a market-based pricing system to all stages of the steel and iron-working process, and launched a comprehensive system of cost control targets set for individual plants, sections and workers.
The targets are backed by tough sanctions aimed at focusing the minds of a workforce reared under a command economy that put raising production levels before all else, officials say.
"If you exceed your costs, they veto your bonus," Zhang Jianping, chief of propaganda for the sprawling steelworks and its 28,500 workers, told visiting reporters recently.
Bonuses now accounted for 47 percent of total labour costs, ensuring that market pressure was applied to each and every employee, said Hangang deputy General Manager Li Huapu.
"We sent them into the sea of the market...to teach them how to swim," said Liu. "To capitalist countries this method might not seem very new, but to us it was very fresh."

Poor cost control combined with falling market prices for steel had cut Hangang profits to just 1.0 million yuan ($120,000) in 1990, prompting anguished soul-searching among senior management, he said.
Profits soared after the launch of the new accounting system in 1991, peaking at 779 million yuan in 1994 before dipping over the next two years due to low steel prices, he said.
Pig iron output soared to 2.35 million tonnes last year from 850,000 tonnes in 1990. Steel production hit 2.36 million tonnes from 964,000 six years before.
GOOD PROPAGANDA, OBEDIENT WORKERS

In nations that allow independent trade unions, a bonus-vetoing assault on salary security would almost certainly provoke industrial unrest, but Hangang officials are adamant that their workers accepted the new bonus system without protest.
Effective propaganda by the company's internal television station, newspaper and Communist Party units ensured the need for reform was understood by all, said Liu.
"Our Chinese workers are very obedient," he said.
Officials said such obedience had been rewarded with a quadrupling of employee average income to 12,000 yuan a year -- far more than the average salary in this industrial city.
Beijing's stamp of approval for Hangang-style reform has led to a deluge of economic pilgrims from enterprises ranging from rival steelworks to coal mines and electronics firms.
In 1996, 38,000 visitors from 6,910 companies and government departments toured the smoky plant with its fire-spouting chimneys, towering foundries and whistling steam trains.

Even officials from China's huge penal network come to learn how to raise the productivity of labour camp enterprises and their inmate workforces, prompting rueful comparisons from one Hangang manager.
"They don't have to pay salaries, so their costs are comparatively low," the manager said.
A LESSON WELL LENT?

While officials crow at the progress made by Hangang in raising productivity and controlling past practices such as rampant theft and abuse of plant property, questions remain about how applicable its policies are to other troubled enterprises.

While many state firms are already deeply mired in a cycle of chronic losses and mounting debt, Hangang's books have stayed in the black since 1978, when it ended 30 years of "losses" sustained under a communist planned economy that saw such financial details as a secondary concern.
The Hangang company is also far smaller than steelmaking behemoths like Beijing's Capital Iron and Steel, although deputy general manager Liu said he was sure all who came would learn.
"If they can all walk Hangang's road, there is great hope for state-owned enterprises," he said.
Hangang officials say the future is bright for their company, despite stagnant profit predictions for 1997 and the prospect of diminishing returns from its cost-cutting campaign.

Productivity gains will in future come from technological improvement, while new financial strategies such as a planned issue of domestic currency 'A' shares will raise capital for essential investment, they say.
That six years of vetoed bonuses and simulated markets have forever changed the mind-set of the plant's workers seems clear.
Even retired company workers who take part-time jobs watching over Hangang's residential districts also work to company-set goals, said pensioner Wang Zhiliang, 63.
"Even after retiring, there are still targets -- but there isn't the same amount of pressure to achieve them," Wang said.
